Changelog

datagoodr (development version)

New

The contents list glimpses the data

Every row of a research guide’s contents list now carries example values under the variable’s label, so the opening page says what the data looks like and not just what the columns are called. The values come from stable_first5 — the first values as the stabilizer will write them — and fall back to the rg_preview sample for a variable the stabilizer leaves alone, which is most of them.

Whole values only: the glimpse packs values until the next one would break its character budget rather than trimming one to fill it, because one complete value tells a reader more than five cut off mid-word. A single value longer than the whole budget is the one exception, trimmed with an ellipsis rather than left out. rail_contents(glimpse = ) sets the budget, or 0 leaves the data out.

A boolean reads as one divided bar

boolebar() draws a boolean variable as a single full-width bar split into its TRUE / FALSE / NA parts — counts and shares printed on the bar in the report’s accent orange, categories named above, and a tenths scale beneath. The scale is the point: without one a divided bar says only “these are the parts”, and with one it says where each part sits in the whole.

It replaces the stack of one-bar-per-category (booleplot(), still the default guide’s graphic) in the compact style, where it is also shorter. A part too narrow to hold its own count carries it above the bar instead, with a leader back to the part, so a 0.1% missing category still says what it is.

A compact research guide, for documentation

create_rg(dgf, style = "compact") scaffolds the same guide as the default "rail" style, condensed so a reader can scan several variables per screen instead of one. Nothing is left out — the same blocks appear in the same order, for the same types:

  • PROPERTIES is transposed into a one-row strip at the top of each variable’s body (paste_properties_horizontal()), instead of a five-to-six row table in the rail. In the rail that table is what set a unit’s height, so condensing anything else first would have shortened nothing.
  • The long tables and the preview are kept short. A block function that declares size, max.lines or max.rows is handed the active style’s values at render time, so one layout row lists 8 factor levels over 2 preview lines in a compact guide and 50 over 4 in the default one. Length is a property of the style, not of the layout.
  • The numeric DISTRIBUTION SHAPE block is dropped — skew and kurtosis are already drawn above the histogram.
  • Smaller graphics and roughly half the whitespace, via RG-compact.qmd and datagoodr-compact.css.

On the package’s demo dataset that is a 35% shorter page, and a median variable of 380px against 610px. The compact guide is the rail renderer at a higher density, so everything that customizes a rail guide — DG.R overrides, a layout.* shadow, a local stylesheet — works on it unchanged. get_design(compact = TRUE) returns its design, and rail_sections(style = "compact") draws it, which also lets one document mix densities group by group.

vignette("report-styles") compares the three styles and shows how to switch, and the documentation site carries the baseball guide in both the default and the compact style for comparison.

A truncated FACTOR LEVELS table now says what it left out

The table has always listed at most 50 levels and simply stopped. It now closes with the tally it was hiding (+ 10 more levels), counted against the variable’s DISTINCT property rather than against the levels in hand — the DGF itself stores only the 50 most frequent, so counting those would under-report. This is the one output change to an existing guide.

The DGF carries a two-axis guess and a suggested stabilizer (formex v7)

formex v7 models a value’s format as (semantic_type, format_style, unit_type) and exposes stabilization as a transform-path search. datagoodr now records and acts on that:

  • guess_* columns capture formex’s route leaf as two axes — guess_format_style (the written rendering) and guess_unit_type (the dimensional/categorical unit) — alongside a human guess_label (calendar {{ date :: temporal }}), guess_match_kind (the honesty column), and guess_variant_id/guess_depth/guess_confidence.
  • desired_* gains the matching target form (desired_semantic_type, desired_format_style, desired_unit_type), and create_dgf() fills a suggested stabilizer — a read :: [convert] :: write plan from formex::fx_plan_transform() — previewing its effect in stable_first5. A reformat the registry cannot reach is reported not-transformable, never guessed.
  • stabilize_data(use_v7 = TRUE) executes those plans with formex::fx_apply_plan() — vectorised and type-preserving. It is opt-in: the default is unchanged, and a legacy raw_to_stable_transform / desired_data_import_rule, where set, always takes precedence.

The flip is additive: desired_data_type/desired_data_class remain the render engine’s dispatch contract.

create_dgf() reads both of formex’s predictions

formex returns two answers per column — the v6 $route (a four-level ontology path that truncates gracefully) and the legacy $guess (a detector at a pass rate). They are complementary, so datagoodr now reads both:

  • The route wins when it resolves to a confident leaf. It reaches types no detector emits — a bare four-digit year is temporal/period/year to the router and nothing at all to the detectors, so year columns are now typed temporal instead of falling through to text.
  • The legacy guess wins where the route truncates, which is every zero-padded numeric key (FIPS, ZIP, EIN) and email address.

desired_data_class now carries v6 coordinates directly. No translation was needed: the v4 dotted vocabulary turned out to be a subset of v6’s semantic_family.semantic_type, so the column already spoke v6.

Two guards keep a wrong prediction from corrupting a column:

  • The storage-safety gate. A number/* route may not re-type a column that .safe_numeric() refuses to promote. The same rule that stops read_as_text = TRUE turning 06037 into 6037 now stops the router doing it. One predicate, both directions.
  • Confidence is not sufficient. A column of rnorm() doubles routes to text/web/domain at depth 4 with confidence 1.0, because -0.6264538 parses as a domain name. So the route may refine a coarse text base type or supply a strong semantic signal, but it may not overturn a type read from storage.

When neither modality is confident the column keeps its base type, and the route’s depth is recorded rather than discarded — a truncated path is a valid partial answer for a reviewer to deepen, not a failure.

create_dgf() is reproducible, and guesses from a larger sample

formex::guess_data_type() draws its sample from the session RNG, so the same data produced different types on different runs — across three builds of the baseball dataset nameLast moved text -> categorical and AB categorical -> text. create_dgf() now seeds it (guess_seed, default 1), so repeated builds of the same data produce an identical DGF.

Seeding makes the draw repeatable, not correct. formex samples from a column’s distinct values and its confidence is stable only when the sample covers them all, so create_dgf() also raises guess_n_sample to 300 (formex’s own default is 100). On the baseball dataset that fixes birthState, which now resolves to mutually_exclusive.geographic instead of falling back to text, and clears a spurious text:web:domain class on AVG.

  • Both are arguments and options: guess_seed = NULL restores the old session-RNG behaviour, and guess_n_sample = NULL hands the sample size back to formex. options(datagoodr.guess_seed = ) / options(datagoodr.guess_n_sample = ) set them project-wide.
  • Guessed types can differ from a DGF built before this change — that is the point, but re-check any curated DGF you regenerate.
  • The larger sample costs roughly what the formex speedup above saves, so a build is about level on time while being reproducible and better typed.

create_dgf(workers = ) additionally spreads the per-column guess over a process pool. It defaults to 1; with the formex fix in place it is only worth raising on wide frames.

Pre-flight check for degenerate columns

create_dgf() profiles every column, which takes minutes on a large file, and a column the profilers could not handle used to surface as a crash partway through, with an error that named no column. A new pre-flight step finds those columns first, and reports all of them at once.

  • preflight_dgf(df) scans each column and returns one row per finding (var_name, rule, severity, detail, suggestion). Rules: constant, single_value_with_blanks (an X/blank checkbox), all_missing, duplicate_column, mixed_boolean_encoding (0/1/true/false), non_finite, placeholder_value, long_values, leading_zero_code and high_cardinality_temporal. On a 568,000-row, 199-column file it takes about 40 seconds; the build took about 22 minutes there (with the formex release before its 2026-10-28 speed-up). smoke_n = 5000 also builds a DGF from a random sample and reports a failure by variable.
  • create_dgf(preflight = ) runs it automatically: "warn" (the default) prints a one-line summary and continues, "error" stops before any profiling if a column is flagged, "off" skips it. The findings are kept on the result as attr(dgf, "preflight").
  • Errors now name the variable. A failure while profiling is reported as create_dgf(): statistics (factor) failed for variable 'x': ....

Breaking changes

Type detection moved to the formex package

datagoodr no longer contains the data-type detection library. It now lives in formex, which datagoodr imports.

The two packages split along a clean line: formex is the engine (one column at a time, stateless — the type ontology, the detectors, guess_data_type(), fx_stabilize()), and datagoodr is the workflow (a whole data frame, human-in-the-loop — profiling, the Data Governance File, review and override, applying stabilization, writing outputs).

104 functions were removed from datagoodr’s namespace, including all 80 is_* detectors, guess_data_type(), score_data_type(), and the AutoType test-case helpers. Code that called them needs one of:

library(formex)          # attach it, and existing calls keep working
formex::is_ein(x)        # or qualify each call

is_factor() and is_factor_df() are not affected — those are datagoodr’s own cardinality helpers, not detectors, and remain exported.

Also moved to formex: the data_type_tests dataset, the data-types/ ontology tree, the internal geography/code lookups in sysdata.rda, and the four detection vignettes (Data-Type Detectors, The Data-Type Ontology, Guessing a Data Type, Formex). Their current versions are on formex’s documentation site.

Install formex with:

remotes::install_github("lecy/formex")

Rule functions renamed: as_* -> read_*

A rule that ingests a written format now says so in its name. as_mmddyyyy() never produced mm/dd/yyyy — it consumed it and returned a Date. The name said the opposite of the function.

The convention is now:

  • read_<format>() ingests a value written in that format. The name states the input. These belong in raw_to_stable_transform.
  • as_<type>() coerces a value into a target type. The name states the output. These belong in desired_data_import_rule.

This makes the DGF’s two bridge columns distinguishable on sight — a rule sitting in the wrong column is now visible without running it.

old new
as_date(x, format) read_date(x, format)
as_datetime(x, format) read_datetime(x, format)
as_yyyymmdd() read_yyyymmdd()
as_mmddyyyy() read_mmddyyyy()
as_ddmmyyyy() read_ddmmyyyy()
as_mdyyyy() read_mdyyyy()
as_dMyyyy() read_dMyyyy()
as_Mdyyyy() read_Mdyyyy()
as_yyyymmddHHiiss() read_yyyymmddHHiiss()
as_mmddyyyyhhiiA() read_mmddyyyyhhiiA()
as_yyyymm() read_yyyymm()
as_yyyy() read_yyyy()
as_mm() read_mm()
as_EIN() read_ein()
as_id() as_id() (unchanged — it names a type)

The old names still work as deprecated shims that warn once per session, so a DGF whose rule cells carry them keeps running. They will be removed in the next minor version. Update rule cells in your DGF .xlsx/.csv files.

read_ein() returns the canonical hyphenated form

as_EIN("12345678") returned "012345678"; read_ein("12345678") returns "01-2345678". This matches the stable form the type ontology declares for identifier / id / administrative (ein), so a datagoodr-stabilized EIN and a formex-stabilized EIN are now the same string.

Bug fixes

  • A zero-padded code is no longer typed number. A group exemption number (0155), a 00/11 code and a zero-padded key (000123) were typed number and lost their leading zeros. create_dgf() accepts a formex stabilizer’s conversion to numbers whenever every value converts without an NA, and as.numeric("0155") does. It now refuses the conversion when every value is a plain number that .safe_numeric() rejects (a leading-zero integer, or one past 2^53), the same rule read_as_text uses. A column that needs real cleaning to become a number ("$1,234") is unaffected. A two-state code that is not a flag now falls back to categorical instead of text, so such a code is typed the same whether it is read from a data frame or a .csv path.

  • A compact date label now reads the run-together form. as_yyyymmdd("20190315") returned NA — the exact case the compact label exists for. A label names the element order, not the punctuation, so read_date() now compiles both a delimited and a run-together pattern and picks per value. read_yyyymmdd("20190315") and read_yyyymmdd("2019-03-15") both parse.

  • read_yyyy() accepts a fiscal-year prefix. read_yyyy("FY2019") returns "2019".

  • read_yyyymm() validates its input rather than silently slicing any string, and accepts an already-hyphenated value.

  • A column with one distinct value no longer aborts create_dgf(). A constant column, or one value plus blanks (an X/blank checkbox, which datagoodr reads as one level), failed with 'names' attribute [2] must be the same length as the vector [1] (or replacement has 0 rows, data has 1). Subsetting a one-element table dropped it to a bare vector, so the frequency table lost its Freq column. The factor statistics, the treemap data and the word-cloud words now keep the table intact; output for every other column is unchanged.

  • Free text of 1,000 bytes or more no longer aborts type detection. base R’s strptime() refuses such input, and both datagoodr’s temporal detector and the call into formex’s date detector passed raw cell values to it. Whether a build crashed depended on whether a long value fell in the first 50 rows (or in formex’s random sample of 100), so it could pass or fail on the same file.

  • An all-missing column no longer aborts the build. Its character statistics failed with invalid number of 'breaks', and its preview was "NA". It now profiles as empty and renders.

  • retype_dgf() reads a .csv as text. It used readr’s type inference, which turned "00" into 0 and "06037" into 6037 before profiling the type you had just chosen to protect them.

  • retype_dgf() refreshes dd_f_levels. After retyping a variable to categorical or boolean the level dictionary kept the old spellings (0/1/false/true) or stayed empty, so the guide printed stale or missing category labels. Labels already edited for a level that still exists are kept; a type with no levels is left untouched.

  • A timestamp column no longer stores one graphic row per distinct value. On a 568,000-row file two timestamp variables each stored a 39.7-million-character cell, past Excel’s cell limit. Above getOption("datagoodr.temporal.max_values", 10000) distinct values, ISO timestamps are stored at the finest of minute, hour or day that fits. A column under the cap is stored exactly as before.

  • create_rg() bakes a DGF path the render can resolve. A DGF outside the report’s folder is now written relative to it (../dgf/DGF.xlsx); Quarto resolves the path from the .qmd, so the old as-given path failed with path does not exist.

  • booleplot() no longer fails on a short figure. It snapshotted the whole graphics parameter list and put it back on exit; restoring the device-derived "pin" it had captured errored with invalid value specified for graphical parameter whenever the chunk’s fig.height was small — which every compact guide’s boolean section is. It now saves and restores only the margin it sets.

Internal

  • .safe_numeric() — the rule deciding which character columns create_dgf(read_as_text = TRUE) may promote to numeric, and therefore what keeps 06037 from becoming 6037 — moved from the (now formex-owned) detector helpers into datagoodr’s own utilities, where it belongs.

  • R/01-06-guess-dgf-types.R is now the documented formex seam. It reads only formex’s public return value and touches no internals.

  • DGF builds are roughly a third faster, via formex. Profiling create_dgf() showed type guessing was 63% of a build and the rg_* data profiles under 7% — so the work went into formex::guess_data_type(), which cost ~130ms per column even for a ten-value input. Most of that floor was input-independent work recomputed on every call (the verifier’s foil-leak loop, the ontology’s own example signatures) plus a 730-format strptime sweep that non-date columns paid in full. Fixed upstream in lecy/formex@3d812d2; with it installed, create_dgf() on the 4,620 x 19 baseball dataset goes 9.92s -> 6.86s and the guess itself 6.20s -> 3.59s. The written DGF is byte-identical — this is purely caching and short-circuiting, with no change to any detection verdict. One visible side effect: formex’s as_integer “NAs introduced by coercion” warning now fires about once per session instead of once per candidate per column (datagoodr already muffled it). Requires the updated formex; older versions still work, just slower. Full measurements and method in dev/performance-notes.md.
